Evaluation of microaeration strategies in the digestion zone of UASB reactors as
an alternative for biogas desulfurization
I. M. P. Castro
, L. S. Azevedo
and C. L. Souza
Departments of Sanitary and Environmental Engineering, Federal University of Minas Gerais, Belo Horizonte, MG, Brazil
ABSTRACT
This study aimed at evaluating the microaeration as an alternative for hydrogen sulﬁde removal
from biogas of UASB reactors treating sewage. The set-up consisted of two pilot-scale UASB
reactors, including a conventional anaerobic and a modiﬁed UASB reactor, operated under
microaerated conditions. Air was supplied in the digestion zone, at 1 and 3 m from the bottom
of the reactor, and three diﬀerent air ﬂows were investigated: 10, 20, and 30 mL.min-1,
corresponding to 0.003, 0.005 and 0.005 LO2/Linﬂuent, respectively. The main results showed that
the microaeration provided a substantial decrease in hydrogen sulﬁde concentrations when
compared to the concentrations observed in the biogas of the anaerobic UASB reactor.
Hydrogen sulﬁde concentrations remained below 70 ppmv throughout the experimental period,
corresponding to an average removal eﬃciency of 98%. Although a decrease in methane
concentrations in biogas was observed, the feasibility of energy use would not be aﬀected. The
eﬀect of microaeration on the overall performance of the reactor was evaluated, however, no
signiﬁcant diﬀerences were observed. The feasibility of limiting aeration conditions in the
reactor digestion zone as an eﬃcient alternative for hydrogen sulﬁde removal from biogas was
demonstrated.

KEYWORDS
UASB reactors; biogas;
hydrogen sulﬁde;
microaeration; energy use
Introduction
The process of anaerobic digestion may be adopted to
treat solids or liquids. It is possible to assume that this
process is an alternative for resources and energy recov-
ery,
for
instance,
converting
organic
carbon
into
methane, the main constituent of biogas. Biogas pro-
duction makes anaerobic digestion an attractive tech-
nology to bioenergy generation and a promising
alternative to fossil fuels replacement [1–3]. Due to its
high methane content, the biogas may be used for elec-
trical and thermal energy generation in cogeneration
plants or may be injected into the natural gas network.
For both applications, the removal of undesirable com-
pounds, such as water vapor, carbon dioxide, and
especially hydrogen sulﬁde, is required [4].
Sulfur compounds present in sewage are not desired
in anaerobic treatment processes, notably in by-pro-
ducts such as treated eﬄuent and biogas. Oxidized
sulfur
compounds
(i.e
sulfates)
are
biochemically
reduced to sulﬁde under anaerobic conditions and
further transferred to biogas in the form of gaseous
hydrogen sulﬁde (H2S) [5,6]. Therefore, the biogas

produced by the anaerobic digestion of domestic
sewage is typically composed of methane (70-80%),
nitrogen (10-25%), and carbon dioxide (5-10%) [7]. It is
noteworthy that trace amounts of hydrogen sulﬁde
(H2S) in biogas may aﬀect energy conversions when
present in concentrations greater than 300-500 ppmv,
depending on the equipment. Due to its corrosive
characteristics, low sulﬁde concentrations may result in
the deterioration of boilers, pipes, and motors [8]. There-
fore, methods that provide the selective removal of this
compound aiming at biogas enrichment are required [6].
Sulﬁde biological oxidation is a low-cost clean
alternative that promotes sulﬁde removal from liquid
and/or gaseous phases along with the possibility of
sulfur recovery [9]. On the other hand, processes invol-
ving either chemical or physicochemical oxidation of
sulﬁde demand high energy and require chemical pro-
ducts, possibly leading to the formation of toxic by-pro-
ducts [10–12]. The adopted pathway to remove the
sulﬁde produced in anaerobic reactors should search
for low-cost and sustainable technologies, thus requiring
simple and robust alternatives, [12] notably in cases of
technologies
that
may
be
applied
in
developing
countries, such as Brazil.
Previous studies [13–17] have demonstrated that
microaeration is a promising technique regarding the
oxidation of sulﬁde produced in the anaerobic treatment
of sulfate-containing wastewaters. The authors observed
that air/oxygen introduction in the liquid phase not only
provided the oxidation of gaseous hydrogen sulﬁde
biogas but also of dissolved sulﬁde present in the
liquid phase. As Equation 1 shows, limiting oxygen con-
centrations favor sulﬁde oxidation to elemental sulfur,
an insoluble and recoverable compound.
2HS−+ O2 = 2S0 + 2OH−
(1)
According to Krayzelova et al. [18], the range of air/
oxygen adopted is crucial in microaerated systems. The
authors established the microaeration range from the
ratio of oxygen supplied and inﬂuent volume, resulting
in the range of 0.03 to 1.27 LO2/Linﬂuent. The range deter-
mined by Krayzelova et al. [18] have been investigated in
anaerobic reactors fed on sulfate-rich wastewaters (750–
4,500 mgSO4
2-.L-1) [15,17,19–21]. Lower ratios (0.0098–
0.001 LO2/Linﬂuent) have been investigated in anaerobic
reactors fed on brewery [22] and synthetic wastewaters
[23], with sulfate concentrations ranging from 84 and
143 mgSO4
2-.L-1, respectively.
The microaeration has been widely applied in anaero-
bic sludge digesters, however, studies investigating the
performance of microaeration in anaerobic reactors
treating
domestic
sewage
with
low
sulfate
concentrations are scarce [23–25]. Therefore, further
studies aiming at assessing the eﬀect of microaeration
in UASB reactors, regarding hydrogen sulﬁde oxidation
from both liquid and gaseous phases are needed and
of great relevance. This technique would not only
improve the feasibility of electrical and thermal energy
generation but would also provide elemental sulfur
recovery.
The main goal of this study was to evaluate diﬀerent
microaeration strategies for hydrogen sulﬁde removal
from biogas, by adding air in the digestion zone of a
UASB reactor treating sewage. The technical feasibility
of biogas use under the tested conditions was assessed
as well as the overall performance of the reactor in terms
of organic matter removal and sulfur conversions.
Material and methods
Experimental set-up
The set-up was installed at the Center for Research and
Training in Sanitation - UFMG/COPASA, located at the
Arrudas
sewage
treatment
plant
(Belo
Horizonte,
Brazil). The biomass of the UASB reactors was due to
the retention of microorganisms naturally present in
raw sewage once the reactors were not inoculated.
The pilot-scale reactors have been continuously oper-
ated for 2 years. The UASB reactors were fed with an
aliquot of the domestic sewage taken after being sub-
mitted to preliminary treatment for solids and grit
removal. The main characteristics of the typical urban
sewage were: pH – 7.6; COD – 515.7 mg.L-1; S2- –
0.5 mg.L-1; SO4
2- – 32 mg.L-1, as shown in Table 1.
The set-up of this study was comprised of two UASB
reactors, as shown in Figure 1. One of the reactors was
modiﬁed to operate under microaerated conditions.
The microaeration system consisted of a peristaltic
pump (Masterﬂex® console drive 7518-10), connected
by tubing (Masterﬂex® 6402-13 L/S tubing, Norprene®)
to an air diﬀuser (ceramic porous stone - 3.5 cm/1.38’’
x 2 cm/0.79’’) installed inside the reactor. Dimensional

The sulﬁde produced under anaerobic conditions via
sulfate reduction was estimated according to inﬂuent
sulfate concentration (see Table 3). Therefore, 1 mol of
inﬂuent sulfate corresponded to 1 mol of sulﬁde pro-
duced. Considering 800 mL.min-1 of sewage and 50

2-.L-1, 0.0004 mol sulﬁde is produced per minute.
The molar volume of 22.4 L.mol-1 of gas in STP leads
to an oxygen ﬂow of 4.5 mL.min-1, corresponding to
the airﬂow of 21.4 mL.min-1. Airﬂows adopted in the fol-
lowing operational phases are presented in Table 3.
The microaeration was applied at two diﬀerent
heights of the digestion zone of the reactor: at 3 m
from the bottom of the reactor, in the sludge blanket,
and at 1 m from the bottom of the reactor, in the
sludge bed. The tested operational conditions are sum-
marized in Table 3.

In order to obtain an accurate mass balance, three
24 h composite samples of raw sewage were collected
for sulfate determination. The results obtained from
the composite samples is shown in Table 4.
Statistical analysis
The statistical analysis of the experimental data was per-
formed by using Statistica 6.0 Software, considering the
Mann-Whitney U Test (nonparametric) to compare the
performance of the investigated UASB reactors through-
out the monitoring period. The results obtained from the
statistical tests consider a signiﬁcance level of 0.05.
Results and discussion
Biogas desulfurization
The biogas composition of both anaerobic and microa-
erated UASB reactors is summarized in Table 5 and pre-
sented in Figures 2–5. The duration of all operational
phases (P1, P2, P3, and P4) resulted in 213 operational
days.
The air ﬂow rate of 20 mL.min-1 added at 3 m from
the bottom of the reactor (R2-microaerobic), under con-
ditions of 7 h of HRT, provided a considerable decrease
in hydrogen sulﬁde concentrations in the biogas. The
average hydrogen sulﬁde concentrations in biogas for
R1-anaerobic and R2-microaerobic were 43 ± 21 and
1,719 ± 477.3 ppmv of H2S, respectively. Hydrogen
sulﬁde concentrations observed for the R2-microaerated
remained below 70 ppmv through the operational
period, representing a sulﬁde removal eﬃciency of
98%. During phase
1, a stable hydrogen

removal was observed due to the air introduction, result-
ing in a biogas upgrade in terms of sulﬁde concentration
(Figure 2).
In the second phase of the study (P2), the air ﬂow rate
decrease from 20 to 10 mL.min-1 did not improve hydro-
gen sulﬁde removal. Both investigated reactors pre-
sented similar hydrogen sulﬁde concentrations during
phase 2 and the presence of oxygen in the biogas was
not observed, as shown in Figure 3. In light of the oper-
ational conditions adopted, it is possible to assume that
the low air ﬂow rate was a limiting factor for achieving
satisfactory sulﬁde removal eﬃciencies during phase
2. Considering the microaeration apparatus used, it is
possible that the low eﬃciencies observed may be due
to diﬃculties in setting low air ﬂow rates in the pilot-
scale system.
Increasing the air ﬂow rate in the subsequent phase
(P3) from 10 to 30 mL.min-1 and reducing the HRT
from 7 to 5 h resulted in unstable hydrogen sulﬁde con-
centrations in the biogas of the microaerated reactor.
Nevertheless, the highest hydrogen sulﬁde concen-
tration observed during this phase was 341 ppmv, a
value expressively lower than those observed in the
biogas of the anaerobic reactor (see Figure 2).
Phase 4 consisted of supplying the same amount of air
at a lower height (1 m from the bottom of the reactor),
resulting in 324 ppmv as the highest hydrogen sulﬁde
concentration. The median sulﬁde removal eﬃciency
from biogas was 96% and 94% for phases 3 and 4,
respectively. According to the Mann-Whitney U Test, sig-
niﬁcant diﬀerences in hydrogen sulﬁde concentrations in
biogas during phases 3 and 4 were not observed. There-
fore, it is possible to assume that the height of the air
supply did not aﬀect hydrogen sulﬁde removal from
biogas under the investigated conditions. That may be
possibly due to excessive aeration since it was expected
that air introduction at lower heights (1 m from the
bottom of the reactor) would result in lower sulﬁde
removal eﬃciencies due to possible oxygen uptake by
diﬀerent pathways along the digestion zone.

In terms of oxygen concentrations in the biogas,
greater concentrations were observed during phases 3
(5.2% ± 2.3) and 4 (7.0% ± 1.9) in comparison to phase
1 (3.4% ± 1.9). Such diﬀerences in oxygen concentrations
may be due to the lower hydraulic retention time of 5 h
adopted during phases 3 and 4. The lower HRT

associated with higher upﬂow air velocity might have
favored air stripping into the biogas. It is possible to
assume that the greater oxygen content in biogas may
have aﬀected oxygen uptake by facultative bacteria or
sulﬁde oxidizing bacteria.
Regarding sulﬁde removal eﬃciencies from biogas by
microaeration, Kobayashi et al. [29] demonstrated that
the use of microaeration resulted in average removal
eﬃciency of hydrogen sulﬁde from biogas of 68.2%.
However, a wide range of hydrogen sulﬁde concen-
trations was observed, ranging from 0 to 2500 ppmv,
probably due to the increment observed for biogas pro-
duction (from 481 to 600 m³.d-1) and consequent greater
H2S production.
Jeníček et al. [11] investigated full-scale sludge
digesters under microaerated conditions and veriﬁed
that biogas desulfurization by microaeration is now a
consolidated technology and the lack of operational
expertise has been overcome. Although the start-up
of microaerobic desulfurization may take a few weeks
for biomass acclimatization and adjusting air ﬂow
rates, high hydrogen sulﬁde removal eﬃciencies may
be achieved (99%) even under initial sulﬁde concen-
trations above 4,000 mg.m-³ (corresponding to 2,876
ppmv). Sousa et al. [23] also reported hydrogen
sulﬁde removal above 90% for anaerobic synthetic
sewage treatment with 0.28%v/v (corresponding to
2,800 ppmv) of hydrogen sulﬁde content in biogas.
In this context, this research contributes towards the
use of microaeration as an alternative for biogas desul-
furization from typical domestic sewage containing
H2S concentrations up to 2,135 ppmv, aiming at
demonstrating the feasibility of this technique for
high hydrogen sulﬁde removal eﬃciencies under con-
ditions similar to those present in full-scale systems.
Concerning methane content in biogas, it is possible
to observe that the microaeration led to a decrease in
methane concentration up to 20%, as shown in Figure
4. Greater reduction in methane concentration was
observed during phase 1, from 72% to 52%. A similar
reduction was observed in phases 3 and 4, of 17%
(P3 - from 64 to 47% and P4 - 59 to 42%), probably
due to the adoption of the same air ratio and
sewage ﬂow, of 0.005 LO2/Lsewage in both phases.
Although lower methane concentrations were deter-
mined due to the microaeration, the concentrations
were above 42%, indicating thus that energy use
would still be feasible.
Results obtained during phase 1 were not expected
since the adoption of higher HRT (7 h) along with air
and sewage ﬂow ratio similar to the one considered
during phases 3 and 4 (0.005 LO2/Lsewage) should lead
to higher methane concentrations than those obtained
during the following phases. That was assumed from
Figure 5. Nitrogen concentrations in the biogas of anaerobic (R1-anaerobic) and microaerated (R2-microaerated) reactors under the
tested conditions.
ENVIRONMENTAL TECHNOLOGY
7

the adoption of similar air/sewage ﬂows under con-
ditions of lower inﬂow rate, suggesting lower biogas
dilution is due to the contribution of N2 dissolved in
the sewage stripped to the biogas [7].
Besides the nitrogen naturally dissolved in the
sewage, biogas dilution in the present study may also
be associated with atmospheric nitrogen introduction
as a result of microaeration, as Figure 5 shows. The
increase of nitrogen concentrations in the biogas of
the microaerated reactor was 19% in the ﬁrst phase
(R1-anaerobic: 21%v/v and R2-microaerated: 40%v/v),
14% in phase 3 (R1-anaerobic: 29%v/v and R2-microaer-
ated: 43%v/v), and 10% in phase 4 (R1-anaerobic: 36%v/v
of N2 and R2-microaerated: 46%v/v of N2).
According to Kobayashi et al. [29], methane dilution in
the biogas in microaerated systems is proportional to the
amount of nitrogen introduced. Sousa et al. [23] presented
a decrease of 14% of methane content in biogas due to
microaeration. The authors concluded that biogas dilution
may also be associated with oxygen uptake, sulﬁde
removal, the residence time of air in the bulk liquid, etc.
Biogas dilution by nitrogen is the main disadvantage of
using air instead of pure oxygen for aeration purposes [29].
Regardless of the decrease in methane concen-
tration in the biogas of the microaerated reactor, the
energetic use of biogas would still be feasible since
its
application
for
energy
cogeneration
requires
methane concentrations greater than 40 or 45%v/v to
prevent operational problems [30].
Methane mass ﬂow in the microaerated reactor
during phases 3 and 4 was in the same range as that
observed under control conditions (R1-anaerobic), as
presented in Figure 6. Median values observed for
methane mass ﬂow of the microaerated reactor during
phase 4 (air ﬂow of 30 mL.min-1 introduced 1 m from
the bottom of the reactor) were quite similar to the
values observed for the control reactor, 36.7 and
37.0 g.d-1, respectively. Therefore, it is possible to
assume that methane mass ﬂow is inﬂuenced by the
presence of oxygen in the upper compartment of the
digestion zone. Nevertheless, future research should
address the eﬀect of air inlet position on methane pro-
duction to conﬁrm the results obtained in phase 4.

sludge

under
overload

It is worth mentioning that high CO2 concentration in
biogas compromises its heating power and limits the
economic feasibility of use [3]. Andriani et al. [3] empha-
sized that energetic use of biogas requires proper
upgrade steps, including the removal of steam, H2S,
CO2, siloxane, and trace compounds. However, Silveira
et al. [32] reported that biogas is mainly used in sewage
treatment plants for sludge drying (simpliﬁed thermal
use with low puriﬁcation required) and electrical/
thermal energy cogeneration with gas engine operation
(high complexity with greater puriﬁcation required) [32].
Biogas composition required for energy generation
may diﬀer according to the equipment manufacturers.
Biogas dilution by air addition observed in this study
may aﬀect and limit the potential of biogas use consid-
ering the equipment currently commercially available.
However, in light of the advantages of H2S removal
from biogas by microaeration (i.e. simplicity and robust-
ness), the development of new conversion systems
considering lower methane content would improve
biogas use, thus reducing energy losses and supporting
low-cost techniques such as microaeration application in
anaerobic reactors, without the need to add a further
step for biogas upgrade [14].
Elemental sulfur formation
In order to investigate the formation of elemental sulfur
in the scum layer maintained inside the three-phase
separator, the chemical elementary characterization
was performed by the X-ray ﬂuorescence (FRX) analysis,
as shown in Figure 8. The peaks identiﬁed correspond to
average values for (S), silicon (Si), phosphorus (P), alumi-
num (Al), iron (Fe), and magnesium (Mg). Other elements
were identiﬁed at low and trace levels. The chemical
analysis is semiquantitative and only indicates the pres-
ence of the compound in the sample. Thus, it is prelimi-
nary evidence of elemental sulfur formation, speciﬁcally
in the scum layer inside the three-phase separator, as a
result of hydrogen sulﬁde oxidation due to air introduc-
tion in the bulk liquid.

Sulfur mass balance
The distribution of sulfur fractions in the anaerobic and
microaerated reactors during operational phases 1, 3
and 4 is shown in Figure 10. The sulfur mass balance
highlights that over than 80% of inﬂuent sulfur load is
lost within the reactor’s eﬄuent, mainly as dissolved
sulﬁde (40–50%). Such results are corroborated by
Souza et al. [5], that have also reported dissolved
sulﬁde as the main content of the eﬄuent of UASB reac-
tors applied to sewage treatment.
In this study, the microaeration was not suﬃcient to
provide dissolved sulﬁde to elemental sulfur. However,
the fraction of sulfur converted to hydrogen sulﬁde in
the biogas under anaerobic conditions (0.6–1.2%), was
mostly eliminated in the microaerated in the reactor
(0.01–0.02%), similar than values reported by Sousa
et al. [23], 0.02%.
Conclusions
The results obtained in this study demonstrated micro-
aeration as an eﬃcient strategy for biogas desulfuriza-
tion. The air addition in the digestion zone of a UASB
reactor treating domestic sewage showed hydrogen
sulﬁde removal eﬃciencies from biogas greater than
90%. The decrease in methane concentrations in the
biogas was observed, possibly caused by the dilution
due to atmospheric air addition. Even considering
biogas dilution, the concentrations reported (40 to
50% of methane content in biogas), would not aﬀect
the energetic use of biogas. The chemical elementary
characterization of the scum layer inside the three-
phase separator of the microaerated reactor showed
the presence of elemental sulfur. The microaeration
did not aﬀect the overall performance of the reactor
in terms of organic matter removal. However, dis-
solved sulﬁde removal was not achieved under microa-
erated conditions. Further studies are necessary to
improve the microaeration technique in anaerobic
reactors and evaluate the pathways that lead to
sulﬁde oxidation.
